title: Hogsmeade in Rain
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 18 of 40
content:
Snape invited me to Hogsmeade by informing me that my boots were unacceptable.

“They leak,” he said.

I looked down.

A dark patch of water had soaked through near the toe.

“They are old.”

“They are compromised.”

“They are boots, not evidence.”

“Everything becomes evidence when it leaves mud on my laboratory floor.”

I glanced at the spotless stone behind me.

“There is no mud.”

“There will be.”

“Is this your way of suggesting I buy new ones?”

“It is my way of insisting you cease bringing damp leather near powdered ingredients.”

“Very romantic.”

The word escaped before I could catch it.

Snape froze.

So did I.

Rain tapped the narrow windows.

He recovered first.

“Your standards for romance are alarming.”

There was no rejection in it.

Only dry deflection.

My heart behaved stupidly.

“Fine,” I said. “Hogsmeade?”

“I require supplies.”

“Of course you do.”

“And you require boots.”

“Entirely professional.”

“Painfully.”

We left after lunch.

The rain was steady rather than violent, silver across the grounds and soft against the lake. Snape carried an umbrella. I had never imagined him carrying an umbrella before and found the sight disproportionately charming.

He noticed me looking.

“No.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“You were about to.”

“I was about to compliment your umbrella.”

“It is an umbrella.”

“A very severe one.”

“It is black.”

“Exactly.”

He moved it slightly toward me as the wind changed.

I pretended not to notice that either.

Hogsmeade was rebuilding in patches. Honeydukes had fresh glass in its windows. The Three Broomsticks had a new sign. Several buildings still showed scorch marks beneath repair charms.

People noticed Snape.

Some stared.

Some whispered.

One man deliberately crossed the street.

Snape's face hardened a little more each time.

I hated that I could see it.

We entered a cobbler's shop near the post office.

The witch behind the counter recognized him and did not react visibly. I loved her immediately.

“Need something waterproof,” I said.

She measured my feet with a charm.

Snape wandered toward a shelf of polish.

“You don't have to supervise,” I called.

“I am not supervising.”

“You're three feet away.”

“Emotionally, miles,” he said.

I stared at him.

He had stolen my line.

His mouth twitched.

“Thief,” I said.

“An accusation from the current possessor of my textbook.”

The cobbler looked between us and smiled carefully.

I felt heat climb my face.

Snape saw.

The bastard looked pleased.

I bought boots.

He bought nothing.

“Your turn,” I said when we stepped outside.

“I do not require footwear.”

“You said supplies.”

“Apothecary.”

We went to the apothecary.

Then the quill shop.

Then, inexplicably, a secondhand bookshop where Snape spent forty minutes pretending not to enjoy himself.

I found him in a back aisle holding a nineteenth-century text on venom stabilization.

“You look happy,” I said.

He almost dropped the book.

“I look literate.”

“Very attractively.”

There.

I did it on purpose this time.

Snape stared at me.

The rain drummed on the roof.

My pulse hammered harder.

I could have laughed it away.

I did not.

His gaze moved over my face with uncomfortable thoroughness.

Then he looked down at the book.

“You are flirting.”

It was not a question.

“Yes.”

His fingers tightened around the spine.

“Why?”

I blinked.

“Because I find you attractive.”

He looked genuinely offended by the concept.

“That is not an explanation.”

“It usually is.”

“No.”

“Fine. Because you're brilliant and difficult and unexpectedly funny. Because you notice everything. Because you can make a potion recipe sound like a moral argument. Because you are terrible at accepting care and getting slightly less terrible at offering it.”

His face had gone very still.

I heard my own voice and decided I had already ruined caution, so I continued.

“Because I like your hands. Because your sarcasm makes me laugh when it isn't aimed at children. Because you looked absurdly pleased when my Patronus almost took shape.”

Snape's throat moved.

“And,” I added, “because apparently I have poor survival instincts.”

He stared at me for a long time.

Then he said, “That last explanation has merit.”

I laughed, partly from relief.

He put the venom book back on the shelf.

“You do not know me well enough.”

“For what?”

“To make that assessment.”

“Attraction doesn't require a tribunal.”

“It should.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It is safer.”

There it was.

Not disinterest.

Fear dressed as procedure.

I leaned against the shelf.

“You don't have to do anything with it.”

His eyes sharpened.

“I mean it. I'm not asking for a relationship. I'm not asking for a confession. I'm telling you something true because pretending otherwise is becoming ridiculous.”

“You expect nothing?”

“I expect you not to punish me for honesty.”

His expression changed.

“I would not.”

“Good.”

“And if I do not reciprocate?”

“I'll survive.”

His mouth thinned.

“You use that word carelessly.”

I softened.

“Fair.”

The bookseller coughed somewhere near the front.

Snape looked toward the sound, then back at me.

“I find your presence…”

He stopped.

I waited.

His face tightened with obvious annoyance at language.

“Less objectionable than most.”

I laughed so suddenly I startled a stack of magazines.

Snape looked offended.

“That is the worst declaration of interest I have ever received.”

“It was not a declaration.”

“Then what was it?”

“A regrettable lapse in judgment.”

“Should I write it down?”

“No.”

“Frame it?”

“Absolutely not.”

I was still smiling when we left the shop.

The rain had intensified.

We ducked beneath the awning of a closed bakery.

Snape opened the umbrella.

It was too small for two people unless we stood close.

Neither of us commented on that.

His shoulder pressed lightly against mine as we walked.

The contact remained.

At the Three Broomsticks, we stopped for dinner because the path back to Hogwarts had flooded near the bridge.

Madam Rosmerta greeted Snape with a cautious neutrality that warmed after he ordered soup and did not insult anyone.

We took a corner table.

“This is dangerously close to a date,” I said.

“It is weather-related shelter.”

“With food.”

“Most shelters improve with food.”

“And shopping.”

“You purchased boots. I purchased nothing.”

“You almost bought a venom book.”

“I exercised restraint.”

“Very seductive.”

He looked at me over his soup.

“You are going to continue this.”

“Probably.”

A pause.

“Why?”

“Because you haven't asked me to stop.”

His eyes held mine.

“No,” he said.

The word settled between us.

Not a confession.

Not a promise.

Permission.

When the rain eased, we walked back under one umbrella.

Halfway up the path, Snape's hand brushed mine.

Then, deliberately, his little finger hooked around mine for three steps.

Only three.

After that he adjusted his grip on the umbrella as if nothing had happened.

I said nothing.

Inside the apothecary, Severus spent twelve minutes pretending the outing had a professional purpose.

He inspected powdered asphodel. Rejected two jars of lacewing flies. Argued with the proprietor about storage humidity. I followed with the patience of someone watching a cat insist it had entered a room for entirely unrelated reasons.

“You know,” I said when the proprietor disappeared into the back, “we could simply walk around Hogsmeade.”

“We are walking.”

“We are shopping.”

“For necessary materials.”

“We have three unopened jars of asphodel at Hogwarts.”

His stare was magnificent.

I leaned closer. “Are you nervous?”

“No.”

The answer came too fast.

Something warm opened in my chest.

“Good,” I said, letting him keep the lie. “Because I am.”

That startled him.

“Why?”

“Because I asked a man I like to spend time with me outside work, and he has spent the last half hour interrogating herbs to avoid acknowledging it.”

His gaze dropped briefly to my mouth.

Then back to my eyes.

“I am not interrogating herbs.”

“You accused that valerian of fraud.”

“It was mislabeled.”

I smiled. “Terrifying.”

He bought nothing.

On the way out, he held the door for me and muttered, “This was not entirely unpleasant.”

From Severus, it felt dangerously close to flowers.

My new boots did not leak at all.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
